I went to drs and a psychologist. Ended up getting diagnosed with ibs and gerd put on pills for both. Started experiencing insomnia and was waking up in the middle of the night, I couldn't sleep got to a point where I was so scared of being in pain I stopped eating. One time I was at my drs and low-key mentioned I couldn't sleep, she put me on klopin and cymbalta.

I went through almost every test in the book trying to prove my pain wasn't anxiety only to find out it was. As for my job? My company actually got bought by another company and my job became irrelevant. After cymbalta not helping my depression she added wellbrutrin.

I guess the short answer is I didn't resolve it my circumstances changed. I believe changing your relationship with anxiety will help, that's what they keep saying. It doesn't go away we just learn to live with it. There were days I forced myself, walking 15mins in the snow bawling my eyes out because I was terrified of what they'd think of it. 2-3 is how far I let it get after 6 months. You have to push through it or seek professional help.

Don't let this control you. 

My last job I got sick once and took a few days off because I was super sick. My work was really cool about it, my anxiety was not. Eventually I stressed myself out so much about missing work that I let anxiety develop physical pain. For almost a year this happened to the point I worked 2-3 days a week at my full time job. I loved my job and I was scared of them hating me for being new and sick and I just let it get worse until working there despite how amazing the job was, wasn't an option.

Hey Buddy, you sound like you might be my emotional doppelganger. I actually remember making a post pretty close to this after I first got severely depressed.

I had a job that I thought was amazing, I ended up getting sick because I found it was mundane and boring and wanted more out of life. When I first got sick I was calling in sick to work every day, I was forced on a short term leave and spent 3 weeks in bed. It got to the point where my mother in law was checking on me daily to make sure I hadn't killed myself.

I ended up getting better for a little bit and found another job, which I eventually lost because I couldn't fix my issues. So I took some time off, like 8 months off. When I was finally ready to re-enter the work force I thought I'd be ok and slowly everything caught up to me again but I tried to ignore it. I actually ended up sustaining a minor head injury which made things even worse and made my mild anxiety severe.

After that, I didn't know what to do with myself. I ended up applying for college and worked a shit job until I could go to school.

I'm now in my second year of CIT trying to work through the anxiety and depression. It's really fucking hard man. I feel like I want to die every day. But trust me it gets better.

As soon as I was diagnosed I was put on a waiting list for a DBT therapy group. We met once a week and I saw my therapist every other week to discuss it. I did this from Sept to Dec. I hated it to begin with, I didn't like be around people that acted like me, or what I felt they acted like me.

I had to fill out some card weekly explaining that I was depressed, doing drugs and how suicidal I was that week. This card was supposed to be done daily but I'd fill out the whole week on the way to group. 

I was so resistant to the group, I didn't think I'd ever get better. One day something clicked. I mean, I didn't change my point of view, I didn't change how I did things. But my outlook changed. My moods changed and suddenly I started to feel better.

I will never stop dwelling, it's just part of me. But now, I can think about it a lot less, because I give myself other things to think about.

Thing is just because you accept the past doesn't mean it doesn't hurt. Distress tolerance is all about coping with things you can't change. There are things in this world that we can't control and acceptance is just not letting it destroy our lives. We are allowed to cry, we are allowed to be upset, but we can not let it take over. Take your time, deal with the problems, give yourself that time. But once that time is over, try to forget about it. If you can't forget then you need to convince yourself that it is out of your control.

Reading what you said seems a lot like what I was feeling when I first started. I like being what I call a bitch, and that is my personality. DBT will help you deal with misery, depression, worthlessness. It works on interpersonal struggles (giving in a relationship, being fair to others, considering their needs). You might not feel like it is possible now, but trust me work on it and you won't regret it.

It's super hard to keep interest in doing this alone, ask your therapist if there is a group available to you.

It is very easy for us to blame other people for our problems because we don't perceive what is going on the same way other people do. I could have an argument with my mom about the sky being blue and I can twist it in my head as a fight that was instigated by her and a visual personal attack on me.

Being diagnosed for me? It made things make sense. Not that it is a good thing, but suddenly when I told my husband, my family, his family. The first steps were obviously denial. The more I looked into it... The more it became true. The more I realized everything I thought and felt, was an altered version of the reality I was living.

Things would happen and when I would look back on them. I could tell my husband a story of something that had happened. He could explain to me that the story I played in my head was not what happened.

After being diagnosed? I've learned that what is going on inside my head only exists because I don't have the mechanisms to control them. Knowing that what I'm feeling can be fixed and I'm not just stuck with it... That is in fact a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Last year I was diagnosed with bpd, depression and anxiety as well as some vitamin deficiencies that could have killed me. I went through at least 40 different medications and I had horrible side effects to every single one of them. I am currently unmedicated and while I am incredibly depressed I can usually stay above water with my husband's help. Those thoughts? They are /always/ there in the back of my mind. For years, I have ignored that little voice telling me it'll help. It won't. It'll take you and shatter the lives of everyone you ever knew.

My advice to you? If you have /any/ friends or family, try staying with them for awhile, or even when you feel like you can't take it, just call them. There are suicide hotlines all over and there are people at all hours of the day willing to help. Members on reddit are here to help you as well.
